clips.title: AWS Systems Manager Introduction
clips.why: How Systems Manager works in one picture: an agent on every machine, and permissions that let it talk to the service.
look: The SSM agent runs on the instance and talks to the Systems Manager service.
The instance needs an IAM role with the right policy for that to work.
clips.after: On a sandbox, the agent reaches Systems Manager through private endpoints, and the near-empty role carries just the policy it needs.

clips.title: No SSH? No Problem | How Production Teams Manage EC2 Securely
clips.why: A live demo of running a shell command on an EC2 machine through SSM, with no SSH involved.
look: The document AWS-RunShellScript and the commands parameter, the same two things the orchestrator sends.
The command's status and output shown per instance after it runs.
clips.after: The orchestrator sends exactly this kind of command, but its whole job is one line that hands the harness to systemd.

clips.title: systemd on Linux 1: Intro and Unit Files
clips.why: What systemd is responsible for, and what a unit is, before you start one.
look: systemd's jobs: starting services, watching them and keeping their logs.
The types of unit; a service unit is the one that runs a program like the harness.
clips.after: Each Nova run lives in its own service unit, nova-run-<id>, created on the spot with systemd-run.

clips.title: Systemd Explained: How to Manage Linux Services Easily
clips.why: Checking a unit's status, starting it and stopping it, shown slowly on a real service.
look: What systemctl status tells you: loaded, active and the latest log lines.
Start and stop as separate commands that return at once while the service keeps running.
clips.after: In the lab you use the same commands on nova-run-42; releasing a VM ends the same way, with the unit stopped.

practice.q: Complete the start line so it only starts the harness when the unit is not already running.
practice.hint: The shell operator that runs the second command only if the first one failed.
practice.why: is-active exits 0 when the unit runs, so || skips the start. With && the logic would be the wrong way round.

practice.q: Which document does the orchestrator send to run shell lines on a sandbox VM?

options.why: It runs the lines in its commands parameter, and the orchestrator's role may send only this document.
That opens an SSH tunnel through Session Manager. Runs never use SSH.
That is an interactive Session Manager session. The orchestrator sends jobs, not live sessions.

practice.q: Put the start of a run's harness in order.
items: The orchestrator calls SendCommand with AWS-RunShellScript for the claimed VM
The SSM agent on the VM, already connected out, receives the command
The check finds no active nova-run-42 unit, so systemd-run starts the harness as agent
The command ends with Success after about a second
The orchestrator follows the harness through its heartbeats every 30 seconds
practice.why: The command is short on purpose: it only hands the harness to systemd. From then on, heartbeats, not SSM, tell the orchestrator how the run is doing.

practice.q: systemctl is-active nova-run-99 prints inactive and exits with 4. What does that tell you?

options.text: The harness crashed and systemd will restart it
options.why: A crashed unit shows failed. Inactive with exit 4 means there is no such active unit at all.

options.text: No unit for run-99 is running, so the start line would start one
options.why: That is the case the check-then-start line is for: no active unit, so systemd-run runs.

options.text: The SSM agent is not running
options.why: systemctl talks to systemd on the machine. It says nothing about the SSM agent.

practice.q: Which of these is safe to send to a VM in an SSM command?

options.text: The GitHub App's private key, so the VM can push directly
options.why: A real secret in a command lands in the account's command history, and keys never go to the VM anyway.

options.text: The Anthropic API key, for one quick test
options.why: The key stays in the gateway. Even one test would leave it in the history for anyone who can list commands.

options.text: The run's task file and its run token, which stop working when the run ends
options.why: They are visible in the history, which is a known soft spot, but they are not keys to outside services and they die with the run.
